summary: Infosys helps organisations build, change and run computer systems, with consulting, cloud, AI, software and routine business-work services.
description: Infosys supplies teams and software to organisations that need technology work done. For an illustrative example, a shop business might want a better online-order system, or a bank might need help changing its software. Infosys and the customer agree what will be built, changed or maintained, and what the customer will pay.
money: Customers pay for agreed work, software use and support under their contracts. Infosys must pay employees, outside specialists, software and equipment costs and the cost of organising the job. Some contracts continue over time; others cover a project. Profit depends on what remains after the relevant costs and tax.
customers: Banks, manufacturers, retailers, communications companies and other organisations. These sectors describe customers buying Infosys services; Infosys does not own those customers’ businesses.
drivers: Projects customers approve, work completed, agreed prices, people and outside-specialist costs, time needed for each job, exchange rates and payments collected.

groups.title: Build, change or maintain software
groups.examples: Application development, business software and consulting.
groups.explanation: An application is a program used to do a task. Consulting helps decide what to change; development builds it; maintenance keeps it usable or fixes problems. The contract can pay for different combinations of this work.

groups.title: Cloud and computer-system services
groups.examples: Infosys Cobalt, infrastructure and security services.
groups.explanation: Cloud means computing resources accessed over a network. A customer may need help moving its programs and information, connecting them and keeping them secure. Cobalt is a name for a collection of related offerings, not a separate profit statement.

groups.title: AI, information analysis and marketing work
groups.examples: Infosys Topaz, data analysis and the Aster marketing-services suite.
groups.explanation: These help customers use information, automate selected tasks or improve their marketing work. Paid use and the work actually completed matter more than a technology label.

groups.title: Reusable software and ongoing business tasks
groups.examples: Finacle banking software, other enterprise platforms and business-process services.
groups.explanation: A platform is reusable software that can be set up for a customer. It can need setup, transfer of old data and support. Separately, a customer can pay Infosys to carry out agreed business tasks on an ongoing basis. As an illustration, outsourced work might involve checking supplier invoices; this is an example, not a claim about a particular customer contract.

basics.title: One bank can buy several different jobs
basics.text: A bank might buy cloud work, software changes and continuing support together. The report can group all that revenue under banking customers. Service names and customer industries overlap, so adding them together can count the same work twice.

steps.title: Agree the customer’s problem and payment terms
steps.text: Set out the work, expected result, responsibilities, price and the checks used to accept it.

steps.title: Put the right team and tools on the job
steps.text: Employees and any outside specialists build, test or operate the agreed systems and services.

steps.title: Earn the fee and bill as agreed
steps.text: Work becomes revenue under the contract and accounting rules. Completing a stage, recording the fee and sending an invoice need not happen on the same date.

steps.title: Collect payment and keep the work useful
steps.text: The customer pays, and Infosys meets support or ongoing service promises. Further work and renewals must be won; they are not automatic.

specifics.title: The currency used can change the growth story
specifics.text: A fee paid in a foreign currency can have a different rupee value when exchange rates change. Constant-currency growth estimates growth after removing the stated exchange-rate effect. It does not remove weak demand or higher costs.

specifics.title: Starting a large new job can itself cost money
specifics.text: Teams may need training, a handover and new tools before the work settles down. A large signed contract can include future years or renewals of existing work; its full value is not immediate profit.

specifics.title: Automation changes both costs and prices
specifics.text: AI may help a team finish work faster. The customer may then request a lower price or more work for the same payment. Check what the contract earns after the actual cost of doing it.

watch: Are large contract wins becoming work that earns fees?
Announced value can cover future years and existing work being renewed.
Read sales, start dates and the amount of genuinely new work alongside announcements. A list of possible deals is earlier than a signed contract.
Which kinds of customer are spending?
A slowdown among major customers can outweigh growth elsewhere.
Compare commentary and results for customer industries over the same period. Check which projects are approved, delayed or reduced.
What leaves more or less after paying the teams?
Prices, wages and time spent doing customer work matter together.

Read wage changes, staff departures, outside specialists and where work is performed. Utilisation means the reported share of staff capacity used on customer work; check the definition rather than assuming everyone is always billable.
Are customers paying for the work recorded?
Earned fees can be recorded before a bill or payment.
Read unpaid invoices, unbilled revenue and cash from normal operations. Unbilled revenue is work counted as earned but not yet invoiced; compare it with the contract’s billing dates.
Do cloud and AI projects solve a paid customer problem?
Interest in a technology does not prove a completed sale.
Look for work in use, what the customer bought and how the company defines related revenue. Separate forecasts of possible future spending from completed work.
risks: Budgets can be cut, decisions postponed and prices renegotiated.
Wages, training and replacing departing employees can absorb fees.
A complicated system change goes wrong
Late work, faults or exposed information can create extra costs and damage trust.
Exchange rates, data restrictions and employee-movement rules can change what work costs and how it is organised.
context: Selling software can also mean helping someone use it

A reusable banking program still needs to be set up, connected to other systems and supported. Check which of those jobs the contract pays for. The software name alone does not identify all the costs or earnings.
quiz: Does constant-currency sales growth mean profit grew at the same rate?
No. It removes the stated exchange-rate effect from a sales comparison. Prices, wages, the work performed and other costs still affect profit.

financialNotes.title: The table groups customers, not platforms
financialNotes.text: The verified segment rows cover industries such as Financial Services and Retail. Their segment operating income must be reconciled to company profit; it is not a disclosed profit for Cobalt, Topaz or Finacle.

financialNotes.title: Read cash separately
financialNotes.text: An industry with high segment operating income can still have billing or collection timing differences. Continue with the consolidated cash-flow statement and customer balances before concluding how much cash was generated.
